title: Sweet and Sour Pork
subtitle: Crispy battered pork in a tangy vinegar, tomato and sugar sauce
excerpt: Pork shoulder is cut into chunks, coated in a cornflour batter and deep-fried until crisp, then tossed in a bright sauce of ketchup, rice vinegar and sugar with pineapple, peppers and onion. This is the Cantonese original from which many imitations descend. Serves 4 in about 45 minutes.
sourceNotes: Sweet and sour pork, known in Cantonese as gu lao rou, is a dish from Guangdong province that became one of the most widely recognised Chinese dishes abroad during the twentieth century. Its origins are discussed in K.C. Chang's edited volume 'Food in Chinese Culture' (Yale University Press, 1977) and in Eileen Yin-Fei Lo's 'The Chinese Kitchen' (William Morrow, 1999), which traces the balance of sweet, sour and savoury to southern Chinese culinary traditions predating the version that became popular in Western Chinese restaurants.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: The pork can be battered and left on a rack in the fridge for up to 1 hour before frying. The sauce can be made an hour ahead and reheated.
recipe.temperatureNote: Oil temperature for deep-frying the pork.

glossaryTerms.definition: A mild, slightly sweet vinegar made from fermented rice. Chinese rice vinegar is clear or pale gold and has a gentler flavour than western white wine vinegar. It is essential in sweet and sour sauce; substituting malt vinegar will make the sauce too sharp and give it an off flavour.

A simple coating of cornflour, sometimes combined with a little plain flour and egg, used to produce a thin, crisp crust on fried meat or seafood. The starch gelatinises quickly in hot oil, setting into a light shell before the inside overcooks. Adding a little water gradually gives a batter that clings evenly.

content.text: This recipe serves 4 and takes about 45 minutes. The pork is fried twice: once to cook it through and set the
, and a second time at higher heat to crisp it up before the sauce goes on. This double-fry is what keeps the coating from going soggy.

The sauce is straightforward but timing matters. Make the sauce in the wok first, then add the fried pork at the very end and toss quickly. Every second the pork sits in the sauce softens the crust. Serve immediately. Use
for the sauce, not malt vinegar.
Toss the {{pork-shoulder}} with {{soy-sauce}} and {{shaoxing-wine}} and leave for 10 minutes.
Whisk together the {{cornflour}}, {{plain-flour}}, beaten egg and water to make a thick batter. Add the marinated pork and mix to coat each piece evenly.
Heat the oil in a wok to 170°C. Fry the pork in batches for 4 to 5 minutes until pale golden and just cooked through. Lift out and drain on a rack. Do not crowd the wok.
Increase the oil to 190°C and return all the pork to the wok. Fry for 2 minutes until deep golden and crisp. Drain on the rack. Pour off all but 2 tablespoons of the oil.
In the remaining oil over a medium-high heat, fry the {{garlic}} for 30 seconds, then add the peppers and onion and stir-fry for 2 minutes. Add the {{pineapple-chunks}} and stir briefly.
Add the {{tomato-ketchup}}, {{rice-vinegar}}, sugar and soy sauce. Bring to a bubble, then stir in the cornflour slurry. Cook for 1 minute until the sauce is glossy and thick.
Tip in the crispy pork, toss for 20 to 30 seconds to coat and serve immediately with steamed rice.

items.symptom: The batter slides off during frying
items.cause: The pork was not patted dry before battering, or the batter is too thin
items.fix: Pat the marinated pork dry on kitchen paper before mixing with the batter. The batter should coat the back of a spoon thickly.

items.symptom: The pork goes soggy in the sauce
items.cause: It sat in the sauce too long
items.fix: Add the pork to the sauce at the very last moment and serve within 2 minutes. There is no recovery once the crust has softened.

items.cause: The ratio of vinegar to sugar is off or the ketchup brand is very sweet
items.fix: Add an extra tablespoon of rice vinegar and taste again. The sauce should have a noticeable sharpness that balances the sweetness.

content.text: Sweet and sour pork is a Cantonese dish that spread globally through Hong Kong restaurants. The bright red colour and sharp-sweet sauce made it recognisable abroad. The pork must stay crisp. If it sits in sauce it softens quickly, so dress the dish just before serving.
